title: The Birth of Jesus
lead: God enters the darkness of the world not from a distance, but by becoming one of us.
questions: In what ordinary corner of my life might God’s sign be lying, one I keep walking past because I am waiting for something more spectacular?
Who around me feels like someone no one important ever announces anything to, and what can I announce to them?
Which movement am I missing: going and telling like the shepherds, or treasuring and pondering like Mary?
note: Scripture quotations are from the Berean Standard Bible (public domain) unless otherwise noted.

paragraphs: Today something happens that our journey has been waiting twenty-seven days for, and humanity countless centuries: the promise given in Eden, that the offspring of the woman would crush the serpent’s head, receives a name, lungs, and a mother. Luke begins with big politics. Caesar Augustus’s census decree brings Joseph and the pregnant Mary to Bethlehem, exactly where the prophet Micah had said the Messiah would be born. The logistics of the prophecy were arranged by an emperor who had never heard of it. And the address itself says everything: Bethlehem means “house of bread,” and in that house of bread the One who will call Himself the bread of life is laid in a manger, a feeding trough.

“There was no room for them in the inn,” but the Greek says something quieter: the word katalyma means the guest room of an ordinary house. Most likely the relatives’ house was full, and the family settled in the lower part of a Judean cave-house, where the animals were kept and stone troughs were cut into the rock. God did not enter the world through a throne room. He came in through the back, into the cramped space and the smells of everyday life, and He cried like every baby. That was exactly the point: one of us, all the way. And at night, over the shepherds’ field, heaven issued a counter-proclamation to the propaganda of an empire that called the birth of Augustus “good news” and Augustus himself a savior: “Today in the city of David a Savior has been born to you. He is Christ the Lord!” The true Lord of the world does not lie on a throne in Rome, but in a trough in Bethlehem. The army of heaven came to announce one thing: peace.

The news went to people on the night shift, just as earlier in this series it went to the lepers outside Samaria and to Naaman’s little slave girl. The sign was nothing spectacular: “You will find a baby wrapped in swaddling cloths and lying in a manger.” Anyone who looks for God only in the extraordinary will walk right past a sign like that. The shepherds went, saw, and told: the first evangelists, with no education and no titles, just a message and a pair of feet. And Mary “treasured up all these things and pondered them in her heart”: she kept what she did not yet understand. The church needs both of these movements at once.

Today something happens that our series has been waiting twenty-seven days for, and humanity countless centuries. All through the Old Testament we have watched God come to people in a thousand ways: in a promise, in a miracle, in a quiet voice, in someone else’s sleepless night. But He always came from the outside. Today we begin the section “There Is Hope When God Comes to You,” and it begins with the night when God came differently: not for a visit, but to stay. Not in fire, but in flesh. The promise from the first day of our journey, given in Eden, that the offspring of the woman would crush the serpent’s head, stopped being a promise. It received a name, lungs, and a mother.

sections.heading: The Decree and the Plan
paragraphs: Luke begins with big politics: “Now in those days a decree went out from Caesar Augustus that a census should be taken of the whole empire.” Rome is counting its subjects so it can collect taxes and draft recruits more efficiently. And it is this very tax document that sends Joseph and the pregnant Mary from Nazareth to Bethlehem, the city of David, because that is where David’s descendants were told to register. The prophet Micah had pointed to Bethlehem centuries earlier as the Messiah’s birthplace, but Mary and Joseph lived some seventy miles to the north. The logistics of the prophecy were arranged by an emperor who had never heard of it. We saw the same thing yesterday with Cyrus, and the day before in Xerxes’ sleepless night: God writes His plans on the official stationery of empires. Augustus was signing a tax decree. He had no idea he was addressing the envelope for the greatest gift in history.

sections.heading: The House of Bread
paragraphs: The address is no accident either. Bethlehem means “house of bread.” We know this little town from day seventeen of our journey: here famine once drove Elimelech’s family away, here Naomi came back with Ruth, here Boaz redeemed the foreign woman and her future, here Obed was born, David’s grandfather. Many generations later, in the same “house of bread,” the One is born who will say of Himself: “I am the bread of life.” And He is laid, as Luke notes with a simplicity that takes your breath away, in a manger, that is, in a feeding trough. The Bread of Life in a feed box. God’s first bed on earth is the place animals eat from. This symbolism is not our idea but God’s: no one else set up this scene.

sections.heading: No Room
paragraphs: “There was no room for them in the inn,” our translations say, and we picture a heartless innkeeper slamming the door. That picture is worth correcting, because the Greek says something quieter. The word Luke uses, katalyma, means the guest room of an ordinary house; Luke has a different word for an inn, and he uses it only later, in the parable of the good Samaritan. So most likely Joseph stayed with relatives, but the guest room of a house crowded with people who had come for the census was already taken, and the family settled in the lower part of the house, where the animals were kept. Archaeology knows these houses well: a natural or enlarged cave, divided into two levels, people above and livestock below, with a stone trough cut into the rock. Animals and family under one roof was not poverty or an emergency; it was normal in that landscape. And that is the deepest message of this scene: God did not enter the world through a throne room, or even through a dramatic rejection. He came in through the back, into the cramped space of an ordinary home, into the smell of animals and everyday life. The Christmas-carol version in which “no crying He makes” has been scrubbed clean of the truth of the incarnation: He cried like every baby, got cold like every baby, got hungry like every baby. That was exactly the point. One of us, all the way.

sections.heading: A Counter-Proclamation
paragraphs: At night outside Bethlehem a scene unfolds whose sharp edge only shows against the backdrop of its time. The empire ran an elaborate propaganda of emperor worship: an inscription has survived in which the birth of Augustus is called “good news,” he himself the savior of the world, and his reign an era of peace. Rome really was waiting for a golden age back then. After decades of civil war, the poets of the day wrote of the hope that an age of peace was dawning, and some tied it to the expectation that Augustus would have a son and heir who would make that age last. The world was literally pregnant with messianic expectation; it just had the wrong address written down: the palace. And now the angel speaks to the shepherds in exactly these terms: “Behold, I bring you good news of great joy that will be for all the people: Today in the city of David a Savior has been born to you. He is Christ the Lord!” Good news, Savior, Lord, peace on earth: title by title, heaven issues a counter-proclamation to imperial propaganda. The true Lord of the world does not lie on a throne in Rome, but in a trough in Bethlehem. And the word “Lord,” kyrios, is what the Greek Old Testament uses in place of the name of God. The angel does not tell the shepherds that a great man has been born. He tells them that in the city of David, wrapped in swaddling cloths, lies the One whose name Israel did not dare to pronounce. One more detail: Luke describes the choir that sings this with a word that means a host, an army. The army of heaven hung over the shepherds’ field and announced one thing: peace. The only army in history that came for no other reason than to announce a truce between God and humanity.

sections.heading: The Night Shift
paragraphs: Notice who all this was announced to. Not the priests in the temple, not the scholars, not Herod’s court, and certainly not Rome. Shepherds on the night shift, people who did the dirty work, who just then were “keeping watch over their flocks by night.” There is one more tenderness in this choice, and you can only hear it against the history of this little town. In the fields around Bethlehem another boy from this village once tended sheep, the youngest of the family, who had to be sent for because no one had thought of him. His name was David. Now, in those same fields, shepherds hear that in the city of David the promised Son of David has been born. The king who had been a shepherd lived to see a Descendant announced to shepherds. We have seen this habit of God’s all through the series: the good news of the empty camp came first to four lepers, Naaman’s rescue began with a little slave girl, and the first raising of the dead happened in the home of a poor widow. God consistently entrusts His best news to people on the bottom floors of society. And the sign the shepherds are given as confirmation is just as telling: “You will find a baby wrapped in swaddling cloths and lying in a manger.” Notice: the sign is nothing extraordinary. Swaddling cloths and a trough. After a night full of angelic glory, God’s identifying mark turns out to be utter ordinariness. Anyone who looks for God only in the spectacular will walk right past this sign. The shepherds did not: “So they hurried off and found Mary and Joseph and the Baby, who was lying in the manger.” And then they did what the lepers outside Samaria had done earlier in this series: “they spread the message they had received about Him.” People from the night shift became the first evangelists. They had no education and no titles. They had a message and a pair of feet. From that night on, in fact, something in the world came to an end. For thousands of years humanity had told itself myths about gods coming down among people, because it carried a longing it could not name any other way. After Bethlehem, new mythologies stopped being born. The search was over, because what people had been groping for really happened, in a specific place, under a specific emperor, and it had witnesses who smelled of sheep.

sections.heading: Mary Treasured These Things
paragraphs: In the middle of all this commotion Luke leaves us one quiet sentence about the mother: “But Mary treasured up all these things and pondered them in her heart.” The Greek verb used here means storing information for careful analysis. Mary was not “getting sentimental over memories.” She was gathering and assembling the evidence: the angel’s words from months before, the shepherds’ story, everything that was happening around her Child, and she was pondering how it all fit together. This is what mature faith looks like in a season when we don’t yet understand everything: it does not throw out the difficult pieces or close the case too quickly; it stores them and reflects. Much of what God does in our lives we will understand only years later, provided we keep the material. And the shepherds “returned, glorifying and praising God for all they had heard and seen.” They went back to the sheep. To the same night shift, the same field. But now as different people: people to whom God had come to say in person that He had not forgotten them.

sections.heading: For Today
paragraphs: The section we begin today is addressed, as its title says, to those who have waited their whole lives, to the defeated, the passed over, and the stuck. If you belong to one of those tribes, the story of the night in Bethlehem tells you three things. First: God does not save the world by correspondence. He entered your kind of life, with its cramped spaces, its smells, and its tears, and He knows it from the inside. You don’t have to climb up to Him; He has already come down. Second: His identifying mark is often ordinariness. Don’t miss God just because He came without fireworks, in an event that looks like ordinary life. Third: the good news starts with the night shift. If you feel like someone no one important ever announces anything to, you are in exactly the group to whom God sent His army with a message of peace. And as a community, let us learn from the first people who heard it: the shepherds did not keep the news to themselves, and Mary treasured it and pondered it. Some went off to speak; one went off to think. The church needs both of these movements at once.
